This verse says that the fate of the Jews of Banu al-Nadir, and of those the hypocrites had deceived, resembles that of those who came just before them, who tasted the bitter result of their conduct in this world and who will also face a painful punishment in the Hereafter. Most commentators identify these earlier people as the Banu Qaynuqa, whom the Prophet ﷺ had expelled before the Banu al-Nadir. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, however, take them to be the dead of Badr, while Qatada takes the reference to be the Banu al-Nadir themselves, before the Banu Qurayza were removed. Al-Tabari holds that the verse refers generally to all who suffered God's vengeance for rejecting their prophets. On the word wabal, some explain it as punishment, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i take it to mean the evil outcome of an act. The comparison with Satan is explained by most, including Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan, as follows: Satan leads a man into disbelief and then disowns him, just as the hypocrites encouraged the Jews and then abandoned them. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari relate the story of the monk Barsisa as a well-known illustration, though al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya consider it weak, and Ibn Kathir notes that it is not necessarily the only meaning intended. The commentators present these different readings without deciding between them.

God compares the hypocrites, who had promised the Jews of Banu al-Nadir support and then abandoned them, to the Devil, who urges a man to disbelieve and then disowns him once he has fallen into unbelief. The commentators differ on who the man is. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, read the comparison as general, applying to anyone who obeys Satan. Many also report a story of a Israelite monk named Barsisa whom Satan led into murder and then disbelief; Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note the weakness of its chains of transmission and treat it as an illustration rather than the cause of revelation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi explain that the Devil's words "I fear God" are a pretence, not a real conviction. As for those compared, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi say they are Banu al-Nadir, while Mujahid and others name the Quraysh killed at Badr, and some name Banu Qaynuqa' or Banu Qurayza. Al-Tabari concluded that the comparison covers both the Jews and the hypocrites. All agree on the final fate of the two: they will remain forever in the Fire, the recompense of the wrongdoers.

The commentators explain that this verse draws a comparison between the hypocrites, who promised the Jews of Banu al-Nadir their support and then abandoned them, and the devil, who leads a man astray and then disowns him. The plain meaning is that the end of both the devil and the man who obeyed him will be the Fire, where they will remain forever, and that this is the recompense of the wrongdoers, meaning the disbelievers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi relate the verse to the case of Banu al-Nadir, and Ibn 'Abbas reports that the hypocrites had urged them to resist and then disowned them, as the devil disowned Barsisa. On the identity of the devil and the man, Mujahid and most scholars take them as generic terms for any seducer and any person who obeys him. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir cite instead a story of a monk of the Children of Israel named Barsisa, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers weak and which Ibn Kathir treats as an illustration rather than the sole intended meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan link the verse to Iblis who misled the Quraysh at Badr, a view also reported by al-Alusi. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the disowning will happen on the Day of Resurrection. On recitation, most read the word for their end in the accusative and al-Hasan in the nominative, while Ibn Mas'ud reads 'abiding' in the nominative, a grammatical point that al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss at length.

The verse calls believers to fear God and to let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, which the commentators understand as the Day of Resurrection, named as tomorrow to bring it near. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take this reading. Qatada and al-Hasan say God has brought the Hour so close that it is like tomorrow, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take yesterday to be this world and tomorrow the Hereafter. They differ on the repetition of the command to be mindful of God. Ibn Kathir sees it as emphasis, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy see a second and distinct command: the first concerns performing duties and the second avoiding prohibitions, or else repentance for the past and guarding against sin in the future. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the forgetting of God as abandoning His command, and God making such people forget their own good as a requital of the same kind as their deed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also mention a reading in which God shows people on the Last Day the terrors through which they forgot themselves, and al-Razi regards this as general rather than limited to those who forgot. Al-Zamakhshari explains the indefinite forms of 'soul' as referring to the few who reflect, and of 'tomorrow' as expressing its magnitude. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith about charity given when this verse was recited, and al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi quote Malik ibn Dinar's words on the gate of Paradise. The core meaning is clear: take account of oneself before one is judged.

The verse means that God forbids believers to be like those who neglected His right and turned away from obedience to Him; in return, He made them forget their own interests, so that they prepared nothing good for their souls. These are the defiantly disobedient, those who went out of obedience to God. Commentators agree that forgetting here means abandonment and heedlessness, and that the punishment mirrors the deed: whoever forgets God forgets himself and his own good. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these people neglected God's right, so He left them without their share of good. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i add that whoever does not know his God does not know his soul and its perfection, and that knowing one's soul leads to knowing one's Lord. Al-Samani and al-Nahhas note that 'ansahum' in the sense of 'made them forget' is hard to accept in Arabic, so the verb is better understood as abandonment. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud also mention that God may let them forget themselves by showing them, on the Day of Resurrection, horrors that make them forget their own selves. The verse then states that the people of Paradise, who are the winners, are not equal to the people of the Fire. Most exegetes connect this passage with the call to prepare for tomorrow, that is the Last Day, through self-examination and the fear of God. Thus neglecting God leads to loss, while remembering Him saves the soul.

This verse draws a sharp contrast between the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise: the two are not equal in condition or in rank, and the people of Paradise are the winners, saved from what they feared and reaching what they loved. The commentators place it after exhortations to piety and not forgetting God, presenting it as the outcome of both groups. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they are not equal in God's judgment on the Day of Resurrection, the people of Paradise being His honored friends. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi clarify that the people of Paradise are those saved from the Fire. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: a difference in circumstances, bliss against torment, or a difference in standing with God. Al-Zamakhshari sees it as a warning to heedless people, like telling a son who disobeys his father that the man is his father. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that the comparison concerns the afterlife rather than this world. Shafi'i jurists cited the verse to argue that a Muslim is not executed for killing a non-Muslim, but al-Alusi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur find this use weak, since the verse concerns the Hereafter. Al-Shinqiti notes that mentioning the people of the Fire first signals that the shortfall comes from them.

This verse highlights the greatness of the Quran: had it been sent down upon a mountain endowed with discernment, the mountain would have humbled itself and split apart out of fear of God, and God presents this comparison to people so that they may reflect. Most commentators read it as a figure of speech meant to rebuke the human for the hardness of the heart and the lack of humility when reciting the Quran, since the mountain, however hard, is more fit to humble itself than a human being. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the fear comes from the weight and greatness of the Quran, which people are commanded to receive with fear and humility, and Ibn Kathir adds that if deaf mountains could understand God's speech they would humble themselves, all the more so a human who has heard and understood it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi take it as an imagined representation whose purpose is reproach. Another view, reported by al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, holds that the address is to the Prophet, who was strengthened by God to bear what mountains cannot, or to the community as a whole. Al-Razi sees the humbling as an image of the hardness of unbelievers' hearts. Al-Sam'ani notes that some take it as a figure of speech while others hold that mountains have a knowledge people do not perceive. The commentators agree on the call to reflect on the Quran, to humble oneself when reciting it, and to remember that the examples it offers are meant for reflection and a return to the truth. None of them decides between these readings.

This verse declares that God is the one true deity, the only one worthy of worship, and that He knows the unseen and the seen. The commentators explain that the unseen is what is hidden from created beings and the seen is what they perceive. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir keep the meaning broad: nothing escapes divine knowledge, neither on earth nor in the heavens. Ibn Abbas, as cited by al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, understands it as the secret and the public, while others take it to mean what has been and what will be, or this world and the next. Al-Razi observes that the unseen is mentioned first because it precedes the seen in existence and because divine knowledge attaches to it first. The verse closes with the names ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim. Ibn Kathir explains that divine mercy is wide enough to embrace all creatures in this life and the next, while al-Tabari notes that the particular mercy belongs to the believers. Ibn Ashur points out that the pronoun opens a passage presenting the divine names. The commentators agree on the central message, which is God's oneness and the reach of His knowledge and mercy; they differ only over the precise meaning of the unseen and the seen.

This verse declares that God is the only deity worthy of worship and the sovereign who disposes of all things without rival, then lists His names: the Holy, free from every imperfection; the Source of Peace, who is free from all defect or who spares His creatures from injustice; the Granter of Security, who grants safety to His servants or confirms the truth of His messengers; the Watchful Guardian over all deeds; the Mighty, whom none can overcome; the Compeller, who brings His creatures under His will; and the Majestic, to whom alone greatness belongs. The verse closes by glorifying God above what the associators ascribe to Him.

The commentators agree that these names affirm God's perfection and His transcendence. Al-Tabari reports that al-Quddus means al-Mubarak according to Qatada, while Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take al-Muhaymin to mean the Witness, al-Dahhak the Trustworthy, Ibn Zayd the Confirmer, and al-Khalil the Watcher. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain al-Jabbar as the one who arranges His creatures' affairs or compels them to His will, following Qatada and al-Suddi, whereas Ibn 'Abbas understands it as the Great.

Opinions also differ on al-Mu'min: al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as the giver of security, while others take it as the one who confirms the truth of His messengers. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note that pride is praiseworthy in God but blameworthy in people, and interpret it as exemption from every fault or from wronging His servants. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses at length the meaning of al-Salam as freedom from every imperfection.

This verse presents God as the Creator who determines all things, the Originator (al-Bari') who brings them into being free of disproportion, and the Fashioner (al-Musawwir) who gives each creature its form as He wills. The commentators agree that these three acts follow one another in order: determination, then bringing into existence, then shaping, though they differ on how precisely to distinguish them. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir explain creation as determination, origination as bringing into being, and fashioning as drawing and giving shape, while al-Zamakhshari understands the Bari' as the one who distinguishes creatures from one another by their different forms, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi give it a meaning close to the Creator. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that these names reveal God's will, power and wisdom. As for the Most Beautiful Names, the commentators affirm that all of them are perfect, and that their number is known only through the famous hadith of Abu Hurayra, whose chains some scholars judged weak, with no agreement on a full list. All agree that everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, by the tongue of its state or by speech. Several also report, without consensus, that the closing verses of Surat al-Hashr contain the greatest name of God. Ibn 'Ashur reads creation as bringing into being from nothing and fashioning as giving a beautiful form, seeing in the sequence of these three attributes an image of God's creation of the human being.
